stories.headline: GOP governor defies Dem enthusiasm, tough political climate to win re-election in key swing state
stories.note: A Republican governor held a swing state even in a brutal year, proof the GOP can still win tough ground.
body: New Hampshire Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte won a second two-year term on Tuesday, beating Democrat Cinde Warmington, according to a Fox News Decision Desk projection.

The win came despite a hostile national environment for the GOP and strong Democratic turnout. Ayotte, a former state attorney general, first won the governorship in 2024 after Chris Sununu stepped aside. New Hampshire and Vermont are the only states that still elect governors every two years.

History was on her side: first-term New Hampshire governors have lost re-election only twice in the past hundred years, and not since 2004. Ayotte ran on housing, pointing to new laws on accessory dwelling units and permitting reform.

Warmington, a healthcare attorney and former executive councilor, campaigned on cost of living and proposed suspending the gas tax. Ayotte's campaign hammered her past lobbying for Purdue Pharma, calling her an "opioid lobbyist." Warmington said she regretted that work and accused Ayotte of presiding over higher drug costs, electric rates and housing prices.

Why it matters: On a night when Democrats rolled through much of the map, Ayotte held a true swing state, showing that a Republican with a local focus and a clear contrast can still win in tough territory.

stories.headline: Speaker Mike Johnson projected to cruise to re-election for fifth House term
stories.note: The GOP's House leader kept his own seat comfortably on a rough night for the party.
body: House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana is projected to win a fifth term, taking close to 60% of the vote against four challengers, according to The Associated Press.

Louisiana ran its House races differently this year. Gov. Jeff Landry pushed back the primaries so lawmakers could redraw the map in Republicans' favor, and any district where no candidate tops 50% goes to an early December runoff. Johnson cleared that bar easily.
The state GOP also won a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that let it effectively eliminate Louisiana's one Black-majority district, which had been drawn under the Voting Rights Act.

Johnson's 4th District, centered on Shreveport and Bossier City, is rated R-26 by the Cook Political Report. His big win at home doesn't settle his future in leadership, though. With Republicans losing the House majority, Fox reports he's expected to face pressure to step aside, with Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise seen as possible contenders for minority leader.
Why it matters: Johnson keeps his seat and stays a key Trump ally in the House, but the fight over who leads House Republicans in the minority is about to begin.

stories.headline: Trump pledges to veto 'insane' Dem bills, pinpoints issue partially to blame for Republican losses
stories.note: Trump says the veto pen will block a Democrat Congress's agenda.
body: President Trump vowed late Tuesday to veto what he called "insane" legislation from a Democrat-controlled Congress, posting an image of a red "Veto" hat on Truth Social after Republicans lost both chambers.

Democrats flipped at least seven GOP Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts, giving them the power to block Trump's agenda, reject nominees and open investigations during his last two years.

Speaking with Bret Baier on Fox News, Trump predicted that after a few months of vetoes Democrats would come looking for deals. He said several Democratic lawmakers had already called him. "They'll send over things that are insane and I'll veto them," he said.

Trump blamed higher gas prices tied to the Iran conflict more than the war itself, arguing voters back his Iran policy but weren't ready for the short-term cost at the pump. He also faulted some endorsed candidates who had fought him in the past and failed to fire up his base, noting he wasn't on the ballot himself.
He credited Democrats with running a hard campaign but rejected calling the night a personal defeat.
Why it matters: With Congress lost, the veto becomes Trump's main tool, and he's signaling he'll use it to force Democrats to the table rather than let them set the agenda.

stories.headline: Meet the far-left socialists coming to Congress next year
stories.note: Democrats' new class leans hard left, giving Republicans a ready-made overreach message for 2028.
body: Democrats are projected to retake the House, but a group of far-left newcomers, several of them Democratic Socialists of America members, could make life hard for Hakeem Jeffries, Fox News Digital reports.

In New York's 13th District, Darializa Avila Chevalier, who ousted Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chairman Adriano Espaillat in the primary, is projected to win. Republicans have flagged a deleted post in which she joked about wiping her hand on the American flag, and she hasn't committed to backing Jeffries for speaker without progressive "commitments" such as Medicare for All. Brooklyn's Claire Valdez, also DSA, is likewise noncommittal on Jeffries.

In Detroit, DSA member Donavan McKinney, backed by Rashida Tlaib, beat Rep. Shri Thanedar in a primary dominated by Israel. In Denver, 29-year-old Melat Kiros ended Diana DeGette's career; she has reportedly called the Oct. 7 Hamas attack an "inevitable" result of Israel's actions, and she also won't commit to Jeffries.

Pennsylvania's Chris Rabb wants to "dismantle the military industrial complex" and backs universal basic income, free transit and "national grocery stores." Brad Lander, backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, left the DSA over Oct. 7 but remains a sharp Israel critic. He says he leans toward supporting Jeffries.
Why it matters: The new Democratic majority comes with a loud socialist wing that's already holding out on its own speaker, giving Republicans a ready-made case that Democrats will overreach.

stories.headline: El-Sayed mocks Trump, Vance and Rogers in gloating victory speech signaling combative tone in Senate
stories.note: Michigan's new Democrat senator opened with gloating, not unity, which may wear poorly with swing voters.
body: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed used his victory speech Tuesday night to taunt President Trump, Vice President JD Vance and his defeated Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed accused Republicans of running one of the "ugliest campaigns" in memory and said attacks on his name and faith don't explain high gas and grocery prices. He told parents to tell their kids "the bad guys lost."

He needled Vance, an Ohio native, about having to swear him in come January, joking "Wolverine one. Buckeye zero." He told Rogers to enjoy retirement and said he hoped never to see his like in Michigan again. He also turned to Israel, saying Americans don't want their money spent on "apartheid or genocidal war."

During the campaign El-Sayed faced questions about alleged Muslim Brotherhood ties, his Israel rhetoric and his links to streamer Hasan Piker, drawing criticism even from fellow Democrats. Rogers, Fox notes, couldn't escape headwinds including affordability, the trade fight with Canada and the Iran war.
Why it matters: It's a painful loss for the GOP, but El-Sayed's first act was gloating rather than reaching out, a combative tone Republicans can point to as the new Senate takes shape.

stories.headline: 'LAWYER UP': Dems immediately put Trump on notice amid Republicans' midterm bloodbath
stories.note: Democrats are already promising investigations and retribution, a posture that could backfire with voters who want results.
body: Within hours of their midterm wins, Democrats were openly promising a wave of subpoenas and investigations aimed at the Trump administration.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, in line to chair House Oversight, posted "LAWYER UP" on X. Sen. Ron Wyden posted a single word: "Subpoenas." Rep. Delia Ramirez named Kristi Noem, Stephen Miller, Tom Homan and others, telling them to clear their schedules.

Garcia has said his committee is ready to move fast on the Trump family's business dealings, immigration enforcement, alleged corporate corruption and the Epstein files, telling Punchbowl News his team isn't "starting from scratch." Judiciary, Homeland Security and new Senate Democratic chairs are expected to join in.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth looks like a top target. Democrats have already filed impeachment articles over the Iran war and oversight disputes, and Jeffries has said Democrats would "run Pete Hegseth out of town." Republican Rep. Thomas Massie also plans to force an impeachment vote in the lame-duck session.
Committee chairs can issue subpoenas and pursue contempt, though enforcing them against executive officials who claim privilege often means long court fights.

Why it matters: Democrats are opening their majority with promises of investigations rather than a governing agenda, a posture Republicans will argue shows retribution, not results, is their priority.
